description: This topic covers the diverse cultural heritage of India, detailing the major festivals and fairs celebrated across different states. It is a highly scoring and essential part of Static GK for competitive examinations.

sections.title: Kumbh Mela and Major Religious Fairs
sections.description: Major religious fairs of India held at specific locations and riverbanks. The Kumbh Mela is the world's largest religious gathering.

geographical_data.key_characteristics: Held on the banks of the Ganges River. The Maha Kumbh is organized every 12 years.
Held at the Triveni Sangam (the confluence of the Ganges, Yamuna, and the mythical Saraswati rivers).
Held on the banks of the Shipra River.
Held on the banks of the Godavari River.

key_associations.extra_info: It is Asia's largest cattle fair, held at the confluence of the Ganges and Gandak rivers.
One of the world's largest camel and livestock fairs, held on the banks of Pushkar Lake.
Celebrated at the Kamakhya Temple in Guwahati, symbolizing the annual menstruation of the presiding goddess.
Held on Makar Sankranti at the mouth of the Hooghly River where it meets the Bay of Bengal.

sections.title: Major Festivals of Northeast India
sections.description: Festivals of the Northeastern states are primarily based on agriculture, nature, and their rich tribal culture.

key_associations.extra_info: Known as the 'Festival of Festivals'. It showcases the rich cultural heritage and traditions of the Naga tribes.
A major agricultural festival celebrated three times a year (Rongali, Kongali, and Bhogali Bihu).
An annual cultural festival named after the state animal, the brow-antlered 'Sangai deer'.
A spring festival celebrated after completing the most arduous task of Jhum (shifting) cultivation.
Also known as the '100 Drums Festival', predominantly celebrated by the Garo tribe as a post-harvest festival.
Celebrated as the traditional New Year of the Bhutia and Lepcha tribes, marking the end of the harvest season.

sections.title: Major Festivals of South India
sections.description: Important traditional and harvest festivals celebrated across the South Indian states.

key_associations.extra_info: A 4-day harvest festival dedicated to the Sun God. The famous bull-taming sport 'Jallikattu' is an integral part of it.
Celebrated to mark the homecoming of the mythical King Mahabali. The Vallam Kali (snake boat race) is its major attraction.
Marks the beginning of the traditional Telugu and Kannada New Year.
Held at the Vadakkunnathan Temple, famous for its grand elephant procession and traditional percussion music.
Organized to celebrate the rich cultural heritage and architectural grandeur of the ruined Vijayanagara Empire.

sections.title: Major Festivals of North and West India
sections.description: Major cultural, religious, and agricultural festivals of North and West India.

key_associations.extra_info: Dedicated to the Sun God and Chhathi Maiya. It is unique as it involves worshiping the setting sun along with the rising sun.
Popularized as a massive public festival during the independence movement by freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
A vibrant cultural and music festival organized in the white salt desert of the Rann of Kutch.
A prominent festival celebrated by women worshiping Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati for marital bliss and a good harvest.
Marks the end of winter and the harvest of rabi crops, celebrated with a bonfire, traditional songs, and dances like Bhangra and Giddha.

sections.title: Various New Year and Harvest Festivals of India
sections.description: Regional New Year celebrations and agricultural harvest festivals observed by different communities across the country.

key_associations.extra_info: Marks the Sikh New Year and the spring harvest. Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa Panth on this day in 1699.
Celebrated as the traditional New Year by Marathi and Konkani Hindus.
The first day of the Bengali Calendar, celebrated widely as the Bengali New Year.
The Malayali New Year that generally falls on the spring equinox. 'Vishu Kani' (first thing seen in the morning) is an important ritual.
The Iranian/Parsi New Year. In India, its celebration at the royal court was introduced by the Delhi Sultanate ruler Balban.

important_facts.fact: Makar Sankranti is one of the few Indian festivals observed according to the solar calendar, meaning it generally falls on the same date (14th or 15th January) every year.
